# PFS Filters

> PFS Filters (pfsfilters.com) sells paint booth filters online: intake and ceiling diffusion media, tacky intake panels, fiberglass and accordion (Andreae-style) exhaust arrestors, paint pockets, roll media, pocket/bag filters, MERV and HEPA final filters, and aerospace exhaust filter media. It is the filter division of PFS Spray Booths (pfsspraybooths.com), a paint booth builder in Santa Rosa, California, and ships within the United States.

# Frequently asked questions

### How do I find the correct paint booth filter for my booth?

Start with the booth manufacturer and model, the filter position (intake, ceiling, prefilter, or exhaust), and the exact width, height, and thickness of the existing filter. PFS Filters can cross-reference major booth brands and help confirm the correct media and size before you order.

### What is the difference between intake and exhaust paint booth filters?

Intake filters clean incoming air to protect finish quality, while exhaust filters capture paint overspray before air leaves the booth. Intake media is selected for clean airflow and diffusion; exhaust media is selected for paint-holding capacity, capture efficiency, and acceptable pressure drop.

### What are fiberglass paint arrestors used for?

Fiberglass paint arrestors are commonly used on the exhaust side of spray booths. Their layered fibers capture liquid paint overspray while allowing air to move through the booth. The correct gram weight, dimensions, and replacement interval depend on the booth and coating load.

### What are tacky intake panels used for?

Tacky intake panels contain an adhesive-treated medium that captures airborne dust before it enters the spray area. They are commonly used in booth intake or air-makeup positions where clean incoming air is important to finish quality.

### Do you carry common paint booth filter sizes?

Yes. The catalog includes common sizes such as 20 by 20, 20 by 25, and 24 by 24 inches, along with many booth-specific panels, blankets, bags, and roll widths. Product pages list the currently available variants.

### Can PFS Filters help with a custom or hard-to-find size?

Yes. If the needed size is not listed, contact PFS Filters with the booth make, model, filter position, and measured dimensions. The team can check available custom-cut or special-order options before you purchase.

### How often should paint booth filters be changed?

Exhaust filters are typically changed every 30 to 90 days, and intake filters, including many ceiling banks, every 3 to 6 months. Both ranges depend on spray hours, coatings, filter area, and the booth pressure reading. Replace a stage sooner when the gauge hits the booth limit or when face velocity falls below the NFPA 33 minimum of 100 feet per minute.

### What do clogged spray booth filters do to airflow?

Loaded media makes the fan move less air. Face velocity in the booth can drop below the NFPA 33 minimum of 100 feet per minute. Overspray stays in the work area, flash times stretch, and dirt shows up in the finish. Change the loaded stage. If velocity is still low with clean filters, the fan, belts, or duct need service.

### How do I choose the right booth filter?

Name the stage first, then measure the opening, then match the media family. Liquid exhaust options in the catalog include fiberglass arrestors, Paint Pockets, Andreae accordion media, and the listed polyester products. Powder panels, pulse-jet cartridges, activated carbon, and PFS model kits are quoted when they are not in the catalog.

### What should a booth filter maintenance check include?

Each shift, read the gauge, look for loaded media and gaps at the frame, and clean the floor without blowing dust around. Each week, wipe light lenses and check door seals. Plan exhaust changes on a 30 to 90 day rhythm and intake changes on a 3 to 6 month rhythm, and move sooner when the reading says so.

### What are signs that a spray booth filter needs replacement?

Common signs include reduced airflow, rising differential pressure, longer flash or dry times, visible filter loading, contamination on finishes, or overspray appearing downstream of an exhaust filter. Follow the booth and filter manufacturer's limits when available.

### Can paint booth filters be cleaned and reused?

Most disposable fiberglass, tackified, polyester, pleated, ceiling, and bag filters sold for paint booth service are intended to be replaced rather than washed. Cleaning can damage the media or change its performance. Follow the product and booth manufacturer's instructions.

### How should used paint booth filters be disposed of?

Disposal requirements depend on the coatings captured and local regulations. A filter containing hazardous coating residue may require different handling than ordinary solid waste. Consult the coating safety data sheet and your local environmental or waste authority.

### How quickly do paint booth filter orders ship?

Most stocked orders are processed in one to two business days. Large roll media, freight shipments, custom sizes, and special-order products can require additional time. Contact PFS Filters when a job has a fixed deadline.

### Do you ship paint booth filters nationwide?

Yes. PFS Filters ships throughout the United States. Parcel or freight service depends on product dimensions, quantity, destination, and carrier requirements.

### What is the PFS Filters return policy?

Opened packages are not eligible for return. Unopened packages may be returned within five business days for a refund, less shipping costs and a 25 percent restocking fee. Call PFS Filters at 855-496-7969 before sending a return.

### How can I request a volume or multi-booth quote?

Have the booth models, filter positions, sizes, quantities, and expected replacement frequency ready when you call 855-496-7969. PFS Filters can review the list and prepare a quote for the actual requirement.

### How does Subscribe and Save work?

Eligible product variants offer a Shopify subscription that creates a recurring order every month and applies the discount shown at checkout. The product page displays Subscribe and Save only when Shopify confirms a valid recurring selling plan for that exact variant.

### Can a customer manage or cancel a filter subscription?

Yes. Customers can use the Manage Subscriptions link in the website footer or the account link provided by Shopify to review, pause, or cancel an active subscription, subject to the controls available for that contract.

### Do you supply filters for aerospace paint booth applications?

Yes. PFS Filters offers aerospace-oriented panels, blankets, pocket bags, roll media, and multi-stage filtration components. Product selection depends on the booth, coating system, airflow, and facility requirements.

### Does buying a filter automatically make a booth EPA Method 319 or NESHAP compliant?

No. Compliance depends on the complete filtration system, installation, airflow, coating process, testing, recordkeeping, and applicable permit conditions. PFS Filters can help identify media for a system, but the facility must verify its regulatory obligations and required performance.

### Who is PFS Filters?

PFS Filters is a division of PFS Spray Booths serving automotive, industrial, woodworking, aerospace, and related finishing operations. The team is located at 1400 Airport Boulevard in Santa Rosa, California.

# Published guides

## How Often Should You Change Paint Booth Filters?

Published: 2026-09-05

There is no universal replacement interval. Use booth and filter manufacturer limits, filter-stage inspections, pressure readings, operating conditions, and documented trends to set a defensible schedule.

A calendar can help organize inspections, but it should not be the only basis for replacing a paint booth filter. Filter life changes with the booth design, filter stage, coating load, operating hours, media, airflow, and the limits in the equipment documentation.

Start With the Applicable Instructions

Use the spray booth manual, filter manufacturer's instructions, permit conditions, and facility procedures as the controlling references. If those documents specify a pressure limit, inspection method, or replacement condition, follow that requirement rather than a generic interval found online.

A filter product by itself does not make a booth or facility compliant. Compliance depends on the installed system, operating conditions, maintenance, documentation, and applicable rules.

Inspect Each Filter Stage Separately

Intake, ceiling, prefilter, and exhaust stages perform different jobs and may load at different rates. Record observations for each stage instead of replacing every filter on the same assumed schedule. Check for visible loading, damage, gaps, bypass, or incorrect installation. Record relevant pressure or manometer readings using the booth manufacturer's procedure. Note changes in airflow, finish contamination, overspray behavior, or unusual loading patterns. Confirm that the media type and airflow direction match the documented application.

Build a Site-Specific Trend

Record the installation date, operating hours or production activity, coating changes, pressure readings, inspection findings, and replacement date. After several documented cycles, the facility can establish an inspection cadence based on its actual operation while still respecting manufacturer and permit limits.

When to Escalate

Stop relying on a routine schedule and ask a qualified booth technician or environmental, health, and safety professional for help when readings are outside documented limits, airflow changes materially, filters are damaged or bypassing, or the process and coating system have changed.

Ordering the Replacement

Before ordering, confirm the booth model, filter position, nominal and actual dimensions, media description, airflow direction, and any part number on the existing label. Send those details and a clear photo to PFS Filters when the catalog match is uncertain.

Source: https://www.osha.gov/laws-regs/regulations/standardnumber/1910/1910.107

## Fiberglass vs. Tacky Panel Filters

Published: 2026-09-05

Fiberglass paint arrestors and tackified panel media are not automatically interchangeable. Compare the documented filter stage, dimensions, media, airflow direction, and equipment requirements before ordering.

Fiberglass paint arrestors and tackified panel filters describe different media constructions. The correct choice depends on the filter stage and the requirements documented for the booth or air-handling system.

Fiberglass Paint Arrestors

Fiberglass paint arrestor media is commonly used in overspray-capture applications. Catalog products may be sold as pads or rolls and can vary in basis weight, thickness, dimensions, construction, and packaging.

Do not assume that two fiberglass products are equivalent because they look similar. Compare the current product record and any manufacturer data available for the specific media.

Tacky Panel Media

Tackified panels use an adhesive-treated media intended to retain captured particles. Depending on the product and system design, they may be used in intake, prefilter, or other documented positions.

The word tacky does not establish efficiency, pressure drop, service life, or compatibility. Those details must come from the specific product documentation and the booth or equipment requirements.

Five Details to Verify

1. Confirm the filter position: intake, ceiling, prefilter, exhaust, or another stage. 2. Measure the actual frame or media opening rather than relying only on a nominal size. 3. Compare the media description, construction, and airflow direction. 4. Verify the product variant, case quantity, and current availability. 5. Review booth, filter, and facility requirements before substitution.

Avoid Appearance-Only Matching

Color, surface texture, or a photo may help narrow candidates, but those cues do not prove fitment or performance. When a label or part number is unavailable, provide PFS Filters with the booth make and model, filter position, actual dimensions, and clear photos of the filter and installation area.

Disposal and Safety

Used filters may contain coating residue or other process material. Follow the coating safety data, facility procedures, and applicable waste requirements rather than treating every used filter the same way.

Source: https://www.osha.gov/laws-regs/regulations/standardnumber/1910/1910.107

## Paint Booth Filter Maintenance Checklist

Published: 2026-09-05

Use this general checklist to organize filter inspections and records, then apply the spray booth manual, filter instructions, permit conditions, and facility procedures that control your installation.

This checklist is general educational guidance, not a substitute for the booth manual, filter manufacturer's instructions, permit conditions, fire-code requirements, or a qualified inspection. Assign responsibilities and frequencies using the documents that apply to the facility.

Before Operation Confirm that required inspections and service are current. Check each filter stage for damage, gaps, bypass, incorrect orientation, or visible loading. Review relevant pressure or manometer readings using the equipment procedure. Verify that access doors, panels, and seals are secure. Remove housekeeping hazards according to the facility procedure.

During Operation

Watch for material changes in airflow, pressure readings, overspray behavior, odor, unusual noise, or finish contamination. If a condition is outside the documented operating range, follow the facility's stop-work and escalation procedure.

After Operation Record unusual conditions and corrective actions. Keep filter-change and inspection records by booth and filter stage. Store replacement filters so media and seals are protected from damage or contamination. Handle coating residue and used filters under the applicable safety and waste procedures.

Periodic Review

Use a qualified service provider for work involving burners, electrical systems, fans, ducts, fire-protection systems, controls, or other equipment outside the filter-change scope. Do not infer that a new filter resolves an airflow, fire-safety, or compliance problem elsewhere in the system.

Filter Change Record

A useful record includes the booth identifier, filter stage, product or part number, nominal and actual dimensions, installation date, pressure reading when applicable, inspection findings, operating context, replacement date, and person completing the work.

Ordering Controls

Maintain a verified product record for each filter position. When a substitution is proposed, compare the booth requirements and product documentation rather than approving it only by size or appearance.

Source: https://www.osha.gov/laws-regs/regulations/standardnumber/1910/1910.107

## EPA Method 319 for Aerospace Paint Booth Filters

Published: 2026-09-05

EPA Method 319 is a test method for determining paint overspray arrestor filtration efficiency. It is not a blanket certification for every installation, coating, operating condition, or facility obligation.

EPA Method 319 is titled Determination of Filtration Efficiency for Paint Overspray Arrestors. The method describes a laboratory procedure for evaluating arrestor filtration efficiency under defined test conditions.

A Test Method Is Not a Facility-Wide Guarantee

A product statement referencing Method 319 should be tied to evidence for the specific product or system tested. It does not establish that every size, configuration, installation, coating process, or facility automatically meets an applicable rule.

Facility obligations depend on rule applicability, source category, coatings, operations, permits, installed controls, monitoring, recordkeeping, and other facts. The Aerospace Manufacturing and Rework Facilities NESHAP is codified at 40 CFR Part 63, Subpart GG.

Questions to Ask About Product Evidence What exact product, media, or multi-stage configuration was tested? Which report or manufacturer document supports the claim? Does the offered size and construction match the tested configuration? What installation, airflow, sealing, and maintenance conditions apply? What records does the facility need to retain?

Multi-Stage Systems Require Engineering Review

Some aerospace finishing operations use multiple filtration stages, but there is no universal stage count or media sequence that can be selected from a generic article. Adding or changing media can affect resistance, airflow, fan performance, access, monitoring, and the overall control strategy.

Have a qualified booth or ventilation professional evaluate the installed system. Environmental, health, and safety personnel should determine the rules and permit conditions that apply to the facility.

The PFS Filters Boundary

PFS Filters can provide current catalog information, dimensions, and product or custom-request pathways. PFS does not represent that a filter alone makes a booth or facility compliant. Request the supporting manufacturer or test documentation needed for any performance or regulatory claim before relying on it.

Source: https://www3.epa.gov/ttnemc01/proposed/m-319.pdf Source: https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-40/chapter-I/subchapter-C/part-63/subpart-GG Source: https://www.epa.gov/stationary-sources-air-pollution/aerospace-manufacturing-and-rework-facilities-national-emission

## How Often to Change Booth Filters

Published: 2026-10-30

Exhaust filters are typically changed every 30 to 90 days, and intake filters every 3 to 6 months. Life depends on spray hours, coatings, and pressure.

Exhaust filters on a booth that sprays most days are typically replaced every 30 to 90 days. Intake filters, including many ceiling banks, typically run 3 to 6 months. Both ranges move with the work. They are planning numbers, not a rule that replaces the booth manual.

What moves the date

Spray hours, the coatings in the gun, and the area of the bank decide how fast a filter loads. A week of high-build primer fills an exhaust pad faster than a week of light color. A larger intake bank lasts longer than a small one in the same shop. Humidity and waterborne coatings can change how a synthetic pad loads compared with a light fiberglass pad.

Write down the day a set goes in and the day it comes out. After a few cycles, the shop's own interval is more useful than a chart copied from another booth.

The reading that actually decides

Use the manometer or draft gauge the way the booth manual describes. If that reading reaches the limit printed for the booth, change the loaded stage even if the calendar still has weeks left. If the face velocity in the booth falls below the NFPA 33 minimum of 100 feet per minute, the bank is already too loaded to keep spraying as if nothing changed.

A clean-looking frame can still be packed in the center. Check the media, not only the edges.

Exhaust and intake are different clocks

Do not change every stage on the exhaust interval. Intake and ceiling media usually see dust, not a full load of overspray, so they often stay in service for those 3 to 6 months. Exhaust media sees the paint and is the stage that most often lands in the 30 to 90 day range.

If a stage is loading in days rather than weeks, look for a gun problem, a missing pre-stage, or a bank that is undersized for the work. A shorter calendar will not fix that.

If you do not want to track it by hand

The PFS Filter Rotation Program sets a cadence from the booth and the spray load, then ships media before a normal cycle runs out. The gauge can still call for an early change. The program is there so a predictable cycle is not a rush order.

Question: How often should exhaust filters be changed?

On a booth that sprays most days, exhaust filters are typically changed every 30 to 90 days. Heavy primer weeks and a small bank shorten that. Light color work stretches it. The booth pressure limit outranks the calendar.

Question: How often should intake filters be changed?

Intake filters, including many ceiling banks, typically last 3 to 6 months. Change them sooner when the gauge climbs, the blanket looks matted, or dirt starts showing in the finish.

## What Clogged Booth Filters Do

Published: 2026-10-30

Clogged booth filters cut airflow. Face velocity can drop below the NFPA 33 minimum of 100 feet per minute. Change the loaded stage before you keep spraying.

A clogged filter does not just look dirty. It changes how the booth breathes. Overspray fills the gaps in exhaust media. Dirt mats intake and ceiling media. In both cases the fan keeps spinning while less air actually moves.

The 100 feet per minute line

NFPA 33 uses 100 feet per minute as the minimum face velocity for a spray booth. When filters load up, measured velocity at the booth face can drop below that minimum. Paint mist stays in the work area instead of being carried to the exhaust bank. Flash and dry times stretch. Dirt and dry spray show up in the finish. The fan, ducts, and heater also see a booth that is no longer moving the air they were sized for.

That figure is an airflow minimum for the booth. It is not a claim that any one filter, by itself, settles every other obligation a shop has.

Exhaust clogging and intake clogging

Exhaust clogging is the common one in a busy collision or industrial booth. The pad or accordion crusts over, the gauge climbs, and the booth feels still. Intake and ceiling clogging is quieter. The supply side starves, balance shifts, and dust that should have been caught on a fresh panel makes it into the wet film.

Bypass is a cousin of clogging. A gap at the frame lets dirty air sneak around a pad that is only half used. Seat the new media so the opening is covered.

What to do the day you notice it

Change the stage that is loaded. Do not keep spraying through a bank that will not hold velocity. After the new media is in, check the frame for gaps and read the gauge again.

If face velocity is still under 100 feet per minute with clean filters, stop blaming the filter. A loose belt, a dirty fan wheel, or a blocked duct can do the same thing. Those are service items, not another box of pads.

Typical planning ranges are still 30 to 90 days on exhaust and 3 to 6 months on intake, depending on usage. A clogged reading overrides both.

Question: What happens when paint booth filters clog?

The fan keeps turning, but less air moves through the booth. Face velocity can fall below the NFPA 33 minimum of 100 feet per minute. Overspray hangs in the work area, flash times stretch, and dirt shows up in the finish.

Question: Will a new filter fix low airflow by itself?

A new filter fixes low airflow caused by loaded media. If velocity is still low with clean filters seated tight in the frame, the fan, belts, or duct need a technician. Another layer of media will not solve that.

## How to Choose Booth Filters

Published: 2026-10-30

Choose booth filters by stage, measured opening, and media family. Powder, carbon, and PFS booth kits are quoted when the catalog has no matching product.

Start with the stage, then the opening, then the media family. That order prevents the most common miss: ordering a clean-looking pad that belongs on the other side of the booth.

Name the stage

Intake media keeps dust out of the finish. Ceiling media spreads supply air across a downdraft booth. A prefilter, when the booth actually has one, catches coarse dirt ahead of a more expensive final layer. Exhaust media holds overspray before air reaches the fan. Those jobs are not interchangeable.

Measure the opening

Read the width, height, and depth of the frame, grid, or blanket pocket. A nominal 20 by 20 label is a hint, not a measurement. Roll media needs the width and the length you can actually handle. Write down an arrow direction if the installed piece has one.

Match the family that the booth uses

Liquid exhaust banks in the PFS catalog include fiberglass arrestor pads and rolls, Paint Pockets, and Andreae accordion media. Polyester exhaust media in the catalog is the AFC blue cube and the Koch SprayStop roll. Intake choices include tacky panels, ceiling diffusion media, pleated panels, and pocket bags, each on its own product page.

Powder booths are a separate choice. Spray-to-waste booths commonly use a three-stage panel bank. Many reclaim collectors use pulse-jet cartridges. Neither is a stocked catalog item. Request a quote from the model and a photo of the installed media.

Activated carbon is for solvent vapor, and only after a particulate stage. Carbon is not a paint arrestor. It is also quoted, not listed with a price on this site.

A PFS booth can be quoted as an OEM set: intake, ceiling, and exhaust pieces for that model. Send the model and the equipment tag. The kit is not a published part number.

Confirm before you substitute

Color, thickness, and a similar photo do not prove a match. If the label is gone, send the booth make and model, the stage, the measurements, and a clear photo. PFS will separate catalog matches from items that need a quote.

Question: How do I choose a paint booth filter?

Name the stage first: intake, ceiling, prefilter, or exhaust. Measure the opening. Then match the media family the booth uses. Two pads with the same outline are not automatically the same filter.

Question: What if the catalog does not list the filter?

Powder booth three-stage panels, pulse-jet cartridges, activated carbon modules, and PFS model kits are quoted. Send the booth model, the stage, the measured size, and a photo. Do not invent a part number from a similar picture.

## Booth Filter Maintenance Checklist

Published: 2026-10-30

Booth filter maintenance checklist: daily floor and gauge checks, weekly light and seal inspections, and when to change exhaust or intake media.

Use this list to keep filter care on a rhythm. The booth manual still wins if it names a different gauge limit or a different inspection. Assign a person to each line so it does not live only on a poster.

Before the shift Read the manometer or draft gauge and write the number down. Look at the exhaust media for heavy crust, sagging, or a gap at the frame. Confirm intake and ceiling media sit flat, with any airflow mark pointing the way the booth specifies. Sweep or mop the floor. Do not blow dust around with an air hose. It settles into the next coat.

During the week Wipe light lenses. A film of overspray hides color and wet edges long before the lamp actually fails. Check the seals on personnel doors and product doors. A torn seal pulls shop air into the booth. Note finish dirt, slow flash, or a booth that feels still. Those track with a loaded filter more often than with a bad gun.

When to change the media

Exhaust filters in regular production are often due every 30 to 90 days. Intake and ceiling filters are often due every 3 to 6 months. Usage moves both. Change sooner when the gauge climbs past the booth's limit, or when face velocity falls below the NFPA 33 minimum of 100 feet per minute.

Do not wash disposable fiberglass, tacky, polyester, pleated, or ceiling media and put it back. Replace it. Bag used filters the way the coating instructions and the shop's waste rules require.

Once a year, beyond the filter

Fan wheels, belts, burners, and airflow switches are service work. A new filter does not correct a loose belt or a wheel loaded with overspray. PFS booth owners can put that visit on the same day as a planned filter change so the booth is down once.

Keep one line in the log for each stage: booth, position, what went in, the gauge, the date, and who did the work.

Question: What belongs on a booth filter checklist?

Each shift, read the gauge, look for loaded media and frame gaps, and clean the floor without blowing dust around. Each week, wipe light lenses and check door seals. Change exhaust media on a typical 30 to 90 day rhythm and intake media on a typical 3 to 6 month rhythm, sooner if the reading says so.

Question: Which filter tasks are not a filter change?

Fan wheels, belts, burners, and safety switches are technician work. A fresh pad does not fix a loose belt or a fan full of overspray. Schedule that work with a service visit.

# Booth brand reference

## Accudraft

Headquartered in Paterson, NJ, Accudraft has built a growing share in MSO collision chains with their MX, Titan, and Italia series. Known for integrating Eaton HMI and Allen-Bradley VFDs for precise airflow control.

Industries recorded for Accudraft: Automotive Refinish, Commercial Vehicle, Industrial.

Accudraft Titan is recorded as Downdraft. Filter stages on this reference: Ceiling 38"×107", 38"×62"; Exhaust 20"×20", 20"×25"; Prefilter 20"×20"×2", 24"×24"×2".

Accudraft Italia is recorded as Downdraft. Filter stages on this reference: Ceiling 38"×102", 37"×64"; Exhaust 20"×20", 20"×25"; Prefilter 20"×20"×2".

Accudraft MX Downdraft is recorded as Downdraft. Filter stages on this reference: Ceiling 38"×107"; Exhaust 20"×20", 20"×25"; Prefilter 20"×20"×2".

Accudraft MX400 Side Downdraft is recorded as Side-Downdraft. Filter stages on this reference: Intake 20"×20", 20"×25"; Exhaust 20"×20", 20"×25".

Accudraft SS Space Saver is recorded as Side-Downdraft. Filter stages on this reference: Intake 20"×20"; Exhaust 20"×20".

Accudraft MX300 Semi Downdraft is recorded as Semi-Downdraft. Filter stages on this reference: Intake 20"×48"; Ceiling 38"×62"; Exhaust 20"×20", 20"×25".

Replacement-cycle notes recorded for Accudraft: intake 35–50 days, exhaust 80–110 days, ceiling 6–12 months.

Downdraft: Air enters from the ceiling plenum and exits through floor grates or a pit. The gold standard for automotive refinishing — delivers the cleanest finish with minimal overspray recirculation.

Side-Downdraft: Air enters from the ceiling and exits through side-wall exhaust plenums near floor level. Eliminates the need for a floor pit while maintaining downdraft-quality airflow.

Semi-Downdraft: Air enters from the front ceiling area and exits low in the rear wall. A hybrid design offering better finish quality than crossdraft without the cost of a full pit installation.

Crossdraft: Air flows horizontally from intake doors or front wall to exhaust filters on the back wall. Cost-effective and widely deployed in collision repair and general industrial coating.

Prep Station: Open work area designed for sanding, masking, and prep work. Filtered air keeps dust contained and protects adjacent paint areas from contamination.

Accudraft models listed here: Titan, Italia, MX Downdraft, MX400 Side Downdraft, SS Space Saver, MX300 Semi Downdraft, MX Semi Downdraft, PRO Series Crossflow, Prep Station 4000. Confirm the installed model, filter position, and measured size before ordering.

## PFS Spray Booths

Our own line of premium spray booths engineered for maximum airflow efficiency and filter accessibility. PFS Spray Booths feature the Orion, Zenith, and Helios series — designed from the ground up to deliver superior finish quality with easy-to-source replacement filters.

Industries recorded for PFS Spray Booths: Automotive Refinish, Industrial, Fleet & Truck, Woodworking.

PFS Spray Booths Orion 27 Semi-Downdraft is recorded as Semi-Downdraft. Filter stages on this reference: Intake 20"×20"; Exhaust 20"×20", 20"×25".

PFS Spray Booths Orion 30 Semi-Downdraft is recorded as Semi-Downdraft. Filter stages on this reference: Intake 20"×20"; Exhaust 20"×20", 20"×25".

PFS Spray Booths Orion 33 Semi-Downdraft is recorded as Semi-Downdraft. Filter stages on this reference: Intake 20"×20"; Exhaust 20"×20", 20"×25".

PFS Spray Booths Zenith 27 Downdraft is recorded as Downdraft. Filter stages on this reference: Intake 20"×20"; Ceiling 38"×120"; Exhaust Fiberglass Roll.

PFS Spray Booths Zenith 30 Downdraft is recorded as Downdraft. Filter stages on this reference: Intake 20"×20"; Ceiling 38"×120"; Exhaust Fiberglass Roll.

PFS Spray Booths Zenith 33 Downdraft is recorded as Downdraft. Filter stages on this reference: Intake 20"×20"; Ceiling 38"×120"; Exhaust Fiberglass Roll.

PFS Spray Booths Helios 27 Side-Downdraft is recorded as Side-Downdraft. Filter stages on this reference: Intake 20"×20"; Ceiling 38"×120"; Exhaust 20"×20".

PFS Spray Booths Helios 30 Side-Downdraft is recorded as Side-Downdraft. Filter stages on this reference: Intake 20"×20"; Ceiling 38"×120"; Exhaust 20"×20".

PFS Spray Booths Helios 33 Side-Downdraft is recorded as Side-Downdraft. Filter stages on this reference: Intake 20"×20"; Ceiling 38"×120"; Exhaust 20"×20".

PFS Spray Booths Orion Prep Station is recorded as Prep Station. Filter stages on this reference: Intake 20"×20"; Exhaust 20"×20".

Replacement-cycle notes recorded for PFS Spray Booths: intake 30–45 days, exhaust 70–100 days, ceiling 6–12 months.

Semi-Downdraft: Air enters from the front ceiling area and exits low in the rear wall. A hybrid design offering better finish quality than crossdraft without the cost of a full pit installation.

Downdraft: Air enters from the ceiling plenum and exits through floor grates or a pit. The gold standard for automotive refinishing — delivers the cleanest finish with minimal overspray recirculation.

Side-Downdraft: Air enters from the ceiling and exits through side-wall exhaust plenums near floor level. Eliminates the need for a floor pit while maintaining downdraft-quality airflow.

Prep Station: Open work area designed for sanding, masking, and prep work. Filtered air keeps dust contained and protects adjacent paint areas from contamination.

PFS Spray Booths models listed here: Orion 27 Semi-Downdraft, Orion 30 Semi-Downdraft, Orion 33 Semi-Downdraft, Zenith 27 Downdraft, Zenith 30 Downdraft, Zenith 33 Downdraft, Helios 27 Side-Downdraft, Helios 30 Side-Downdraft, Helios 33 Side-Downdraft, Orion Prep Station. Confirm the installed model, filter position, and measured size before ordering.

Koch BioMAX HEPA filters are manufactured for high-efficiency commercial and industrial air-filtration systems. Koch identifies hospitals, clean rooms, pharmaceutical plants, and other systems where clean air protects people, processes, and equipment as common product-family applications.

The configured item is a 99.99% filter with actual dimensions of 23.375 × 23.375 × 11.5 inches, a double-turned-flange 18-gauge galvanized-steel frame, polyurethane foam sealant, and one filter per carton.

High-efficiency media produced from submicron glass fibers formed into a water-resistant, high-density paper mat.

Precision corrugated aluminum separators maintain pleat spacing and airflow through the media pack.

The media pack is sealed to the cell-side frame with a polyurethane foam bond.

Koch literature lists a downstream neoprene gasket as the standard BioMAX arrangement; confirm the gasket arrangement required by your housing before ordering.

The supplied BioMAX specification calls for a minimum overall efficiency of 99.99% PAO on 0.3 micrometer particles. It describes ultrafine fiberglass media formed into a high-density, water-repellent paper; pleated construction; adhesive-bead pleat spacing; a sealed media pack; UL classification; and a label recording manufacturer, airflow direction, penetration, initial resistance, and test airflow capacity.

Important item-specific note: the generic supplied specification references 26-gauge galvanized cell sides, while the requested PFS-HBM232311 configuration is listed as 18-gauge galvanized DTF. This product page uses the requested 18-gauge item configuration. Confirm any project specification or submittal requirement before purchase.
